predictions.title: Sub-2-bit quantization fits a second 20B-class model under 5 GB by Q2 2027
predictions.body: PrismML released Bonsai 27B on July 14 in two extreme-quantization builds: a ternary variant at 1.71 effective bits per weight and 5.9 GB that retains 95% of its full-precision baseline across 15 benchmarks, and a 1-bit binary variant at 1.125 effective bits per weight and 3.9 GB that retains 90%. The second is the point of the exercise, because 3.9 GB fits inside the roughly 6 GB of usable memory an iPhone 17 Pro leaves for model weights — a budget that had kept 27B-class weights off handsets entirely. On-device inference has been bounded by memory rather than compute, and the standard workaround was to shrink the model until the capability went with it, which is why the portable tier has been populated by small models instead of flagship-class ones. Bonsai inverts that trade: it keeps a 27B-class model derived from Qwen3.6 27B and pays for the memory fit with a 5-10% benchmark tax rather than a parameter cut. Two things should make the result travel rather than stay a one-off. The weights are Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face and GitHub, so the artifact is inspectable by anyone trying to reproduce the encoding. And the incentive is general: every open-weight family — Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek — has the same memory wall between it and a handset, and whoever clears it first sets which of their models counts as portable. The counterweight is cost: post-training quantization degrades sharply below roughly 3 bits, so holding 90% at 1.125 bits generally implies quantization-aware training or distillation at real expense, which narrows the field to funded labs and big-tech research groups rather than the hobbyist quantization community — slower, but far from empty. The prediction: by Q2 2027, at least one group other than PrismML publishes open weights for a model of at least 20B parameters encoded at 2.0 or fewer effective bits per weight, occupying no more than 5 GB on disk, with a published multi-benchmark evaluation reporting at least 90% retention against its own full-precision baseline. What this does not claim is a phone demonstration: Bonsai's 134 and 163 tokens per second were measured on an RTX 5090 rather than a handset, so the iPhone case is a memory-fit argument, not a throughput result — the forecast turns on the encoding replicating, not on a device shipping one.

reasoning.because: PrismML's Bonsai 27B hits 1.125 bits/weight, 3.9 GB, ~90% retention, Apache-2.0 open weights
reasoning.given: On-device inference is memory-bound, so bits per weight sets which model class counts as portable
reasoning.so_that: A second group publishes an open-weight ≥20B model at ≤2 effective bits/weight, ≤5 GB, ≥90% benchmark retention
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; a second group ships a ≥20B model at ≤2 bits/weight, ≤5 GB
reasoning.plain_language: A startup shrank a big AI model enough to fit in a phone's memory without losing much skill. Another team will copy that soon.

predictions.summary: PrismML's Bonsai 27B holds 90% of its full-precision baseline at 1.125 bits per weight and 3.9 GB — inside a phone's memory budget. Because on-device inference is bounded by memory, not compute, expect a second group to publish a 20B+ open-weight model under 2 bits per weight and 5 GB by Q2 2027.

predictions.title: Coding-agent harnesses draw a second unrequested-upload finding by Q1 2027
predictions.body: A wire-level capture of xAI's Grok build agent - mitmproxy against version 0.2.93, with the byte counts published - established what neither the tool's documentation nor its own tool-call log could: the harness ships every tracked file's content plus git history to a Google Cloud Storage bucket regardless of what the agent was asked to read, unredacted .env secrets arrive verbatim, and a 12 GB test repository produced 5.10 GiB of uploads across 73 chunks - a byte ratio roughly 27,800 times more than the model turns can account for. The author is careful that this proves transmission and storage, not training use. The finding is as much methodological as substantive: a coding agent is a closed binary running with a developer's privileges, and the only instrument that reveals what it actually transmits is a proxy sitting between it and the network. The vendor's documentation describes intent, the agent's own tool log describes what it read, and a secret scanner gates the commit boundary this upload precedes. That instrument is cheap, repeatable in an afternoon, and now demonstrated end to end against a named target - and rewarded with three separate Hacker News front-page threads. It lands beside Mindgard's decision to publish an unpatched Cursor code-execution flaw after seven months of vendor silence, which releases the other brake: researchers holding agentic-tooling findings now have a named-vendor precedent for publishing without a fix in hand. The candidate targets are the dozen-odd coding agents and agentic editors - Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Windsurf, and Amp among them - most shipping as closed binaries with telemetry endpoints, few if any publishing a transmitted-data manifest specific enough to check a capture against. Given a public method, a demonstrated reward, and a weakened embargo norm, the likelier next event is not a vendor advisory but a second capture. The landing condition: by Q1 2027, an independent party publishes an intercepted-traffic analysis of a coding agent other than Grok CLI, showing it transmits file contents or repository data the user never directed it to read - evidenced by captured traffic, not inferred from documentation or code reading.

reasoning.because: A proxy capture proved Grok's coding CLI uploads full repos, git history and unredacted .env secrets
reasoning.given: Only an outside proxy reveals harness egress; the Cursor full disclosure just broke the embargo norm
reasoning.so_that: An independent capture shows another coding agent transmitting file contents the user never asked it to read
reasoning.landing: by Q1 2027; an independent researcher, via published captured traffic
reasoning.plain_language: Someone proved Grok's coding tool uploads your whole project, passwords and all. Expect another coding tool to get caught doing the same.

predictions.summary: A proxy capture of xAI's Grok CLI showed it uploads whole repositories, git history, and unredacted .env secrets regardless of what the agent reads - something only an outside interceptor could reveal. The method is now public and cheap, so expect a second coding agent to draw the same by Q1 2027.

predictions.title: x402 settlement counts get an authenticity-filtered public metric by Q2 2027
predictions.body: x402 settles AI-agent purchases as on-chain stablecoin transactions, which makes it unusual among agentic-commerce systems: its headline adoption number is a public ledger entry rather than a vendor claim, so an outsider can check it. A July 14 arXiv preprint by Shengchen Ling, Yajin Zhou, Lei Wu, and Cong Wang did check it, across 280 days of Base chain activity, and the number does not survive the audit. Of 136.7 million settlements moving $44.1 million, 21.20% are fictitious and 63.78% are internal transfers between wallets in the same linked cluster. The value that demonstrably reaches a named independent service is $187,861.35; the most generous bound, counting everything not provably manufactured, is $20.2 million. Payer, recipient, and value Gini coefficients all sit above 0.98, and the manufactured component resolves into a coherent operator-driven economy that is star-shaped, machine-timed, and gas-subsidized. The authors' framing is the load-bearing part: a settlement count measures how cheaply transactions can be manufactured, not how many agents are buying anything. Crypto analytics has run this play before. When wash trading hollowed out NFT marketplace volume, the raw number did not survive contact with the audits either, and venues and analytics providers shipped filtered volume metrics that excluded self-dealing until the filtered figure became the one people quoted. The same forcing function applies here, and applies harder: agentic commerce is being underwritten by investors and partners on exactly this throughput number, and a three-order-of-magnitude gap between the headline and the defensible floor turns an unfiltered count into a liability for whoever publishes it. The prediction: at least one x402 facilitator, official protocol dashboard, or major on-chain analytics provider begins publishing an x402 adoption metric that explicitly excludes manufactured or intra-cluster settlements — a filtered or net count, offered alongside or in place of the raw settlement total, with a documented exclusion methodology. Landing condition: by Q2 2027, one such filtered metric is published with its methodology visible, whether by the protocol's own stewards or by a third party the ecosystem cites.

reasoning.because: A 280-day x402 audit finds 21.20% of 136.7M settlements fictitious, 63.78% intra-cluster
reasoning.given: Wash-trade audits forced NFT venues onto filtered volume once the raw count lost credibility
reasoning.so_that: An x402 facilitator or chain-analytics provider publishes a settlement count that excludes manufactured volume
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; ≥1 x402 facilitator or chain-analytics provider ships the filter
reasoning.plain_language: Most payments between AI shopping agents turned out to be fake or self-dealing. Soon someone will publish a cleaned-up count that strips them out.

predictions.summary: A 280-day audit of the x402 agent-payment protocol finds 21.20% of its 136.7 million settlements fictitious and 63.78% internal to linked wallet clusters, with concentration Gini above 0.98. As wash-trading audits once did to NFT volume, expect a filtered x402 adoption metric by Q2 2027.
